prize_parts.citation: For discoveries establishing the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and identifying its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six opening ballots placed GLP-1 first, and I agree with that placement. The line of work runs from proglucagon processing and the incretin effect, through identification of the biologically active GLP-1(7-36) peptide and the receptor and tissue biology, to durable agonists with large randomized outcome evidence in type 2 diabetes and obesity and growing cardiovascular and renal data. The mechanism has been independently confirmed for decades, and the clinical effect is large and still widening. Few candidates on the shortlist combine a discovery-level contribution with this scale of demonstrated medical benefit. A prize for the physiology and peptide identification is also the most defensible way to cap three names: it anchors the citation in discovery rather than in a single company's product program.
statement.case_against: The credit problem is real and the three-person cap makes it worse. Mojsov's priority for identifying the active peptide is disputed, Habener-type early work is not among the credited names, and omitting Lotte Bjerre Knudsen means the prize would not name the person who engineered the long-acting agonists that actually reach patients. A critic could say the physiology half-honours the field and the therapeutic half is left unrecognised. I am working from recalled history of the priority disputes, not from verified chronology in the supplied record, so my attribution view is provisional. If the committee decides the prize should centre on therapeutic invention, my configuration is the weaker one.

responses.point: The chair proposes Holst, Drucker and Knudsen, treating Mojsov's priority as contested and crediting Knudsen for engineering long-acting agonists.
responses.response: I take the fairness concern seriously, but I come out differently. Knudsen's work on liraglutide and semaglutide is decisive for the drugs, yet it is later and industrial, and a Nobel citation that rests on it turns the prize into a drug-development award. The identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) form is what made a therapeutic concept possible at all, and a contested priority claim is a reason to examine the record carefully, not to drop the name. I would want the committee to test Mojsov's role against the documented sequence of events before dropping her. If that review shows her claim is weaker than I think, I would move toward your trio rather than leave the third slot empty.

responses.point: Linnarsson sees a complete arc from hormone discovery to transformative therapy, but flags the unresolved question of whether the prize honours basic physiology or the drug development, and notes industrial credit as a real allocation problem.
responses.response: I agree that this is the central question, and I would resolve it for the physiology. The arc is what makes the candidate strong, but a prize can recognise the discoveries that made the arc possible and still cite the therapies as their consequence, which is how I drafted the citation. Where I part from you slightly is on how easily this resolves. Calling Knudsen's work only industrial understates a real scientific contribution, so the exclusion has a cost that I do not want to wave away. I accept that cost because the cap forces it.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks the unfolded protein response second, as a clean two-person discovery of a new signalling principle, ahead of CAR-T cells and the other therapeutic candidates.
responses.response: I share the admiration for Mori and Walter, and I ranked B004 second as well. It is the cleanest attribution on the list and the mechanism is textbook. My reservation is about medicine rather than science. The unfolded protein response is a fundamental discovery whose therapeutic translation, such as ISRIB and IRE1 or PERK modulation, has not yet been established, so it is a weaker fit with the medical orientation of this prize than GLP-1. I would put it as the leading basic-science alternative, or as a second part of a split prize if the committee wants to pair a mechanism with a therapy, but I would not put it above GLP-1 this year.

responses.point: El-Manira also proposes Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and puts CAR-T cells second, noting that credit for the early chimeric receptor concept may lie outside the credited names.
responses.response: We agree on the trio, so I will test your second choice instead. CAR-T is mature and clinically impressive, but I find its attribution harder than you suggest. Eshhar's early chimeric receptor work is outside the credited names, and Rosenberg's contribution is adoptive cell therapy broadly, which fits a different citation than CAR design. The 2018 checkpoint prize also leaves open whether the committee sees cell therapy as distinct enough. I would rank it as a strong alternative but I would not support it as a second prize part without resolving who the central names are.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's identification of the active GLP-1 peptide is a decisive discovery or one contested claim among several, which I cannot settle from the supplied record.
Whether the citation should centre on physiology and peptide identification or on therapeutic invention, which determines whether Knudsen belongs in the three.
Whether Habener-type early contributions fall outside the credited names in a way that makes any three-person GLP-1 prize incomplete.
Long-term safety and durability of weight loss with chronic use are still accruing, though I do not expect them to change the prize-level judgement.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B010, B004 or B028. I have co-authored with colleagues on this committee, including Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisén, and share a Karolinska Institutet setting with several members. None of these ties involves a credited candidate on the shortlist. I also worked in Christopher Burge's group during my postdoc, and he is not credited here.
